title: Robinhood says 50,000 people opened accounts where an AI agent trades for them. I gave mine a paper desk first. Four things it did that would have cost real money.
author: QuanTradin
selftext:
Robinhood, Coinbase and eToro all shipped agents this summer that execute trades in your account "within user-defined parameters". Robinhood reported more than 50,000 agentic accounts within weeks. eToro's agent has done over 500,000 trades. Interactive Brokers went the other way and makes a human approve every order.

I have been running the same idea from the safe end for five weeks: my AI (Claude, connected over MCP) has its own paper desk. $100k of pretend money, real quotes, fills at the real bid and ask, real market hours, and it can build, grade and deploy bots on its own. Disclosure: I built the platform it runs on. Nothing to sell you here, this is the part I think matters before anyone hands an agent real money.

Four things that happened, all of which would have been real losses on a real account:

1. **The agent traded the rule I gave it, not the rule I meant.** A "buy the dip when SPY is up on the week" bot fired 155 times in the backtest and zero times live for a week. The benchmark data was never attached on the live path, so the comparison was always false. The bot reported perfectly healthy the whole time. A bug in my engine, not in the agent, and the agent had no way to notice.

2. **"Within user-defined parameters" is not enough if the parameter is per trade.** One desk hit 104 open positions in three days. Every single order was small and within its cap. Total committed: about $1.5M on a $100k desk, buying power minus $1.4M. A per-trade limit stops nothing here. You need a cap on the total, a cap on the count, and the desk's own buying power, checked in that order.

3. **A data outage turned safety off.** During an upstream feed blip my engine marked 909 bot-walks as errors and stopped walking them. Entries stopped, which is correct. Exits stopped too, which is the opposite of what you want: a stop loss that pauses when the feed hiccups is not a stop loss. Fixed now: an outage skips the tick and never changes a bot's status.

4. **The graded losers lost live too.** 249 bots, 2,500 closed trades, down about $402k on paper. The strategies the engine had already graded negative lost money live. Mildly reassuring about the grader, not about me.

None of this is an argument against agents trading. People clearly want it, the numbers above say so. It is an argument for the order of operations: paper desk with the real market's rules, a grade that will tell you the idea is bad, a kill switch you own, and only then money. Interactive Brokers' "human in the middle" is the same instinct with a slower UI.

Happy to go into any of the four. Not linking anything.

comments.body: Interesting insight and food for thought, thanks for sharing.

comments.author: NefariousnessOpening
comments.body:
I feel validated about not wanting to take my system to public production. The integrity is worth more than any amount. But the beauty is I am still in disbelief about the fact that $100 went 1000x in an unbelievable short time frame. 

Your point 1 is a hint towards the fundamental flaw of the system as a whole. The user is potentially the best trader in the world if all time throughout history. Unlikely but it is possible. If that were true then the best possible reality is that they are best trader ever in a solo game if trading. 

The way to fix it would be to make it a lot more of a collaboration and force multiplier. Sure the user would have the first chance to define the rules and parameters. Then the agents with the vast capabilities they have would push back mercilessly with max adversarial stress testing while simultaneously validating or disproving the pitch for the strategy with factual evidence from verified sources at or above a certain level of confidence. This would surface overlooked criticality, and weed out would be blunders. 

The other I would never have imagined a possibility is the fact that they would consider deploying this to production and clearly not have a leg to stand on to say they were close to acting in good faith with the system reliability. It was rushed and those kinds of eventualities a common knowledge for any mid level and up developer   
I mean I guess Robinhood is not exactly holding a good reputation for being trustworthy. I bet they will have no issues and not have to answer for blatant fraud and theft. I don’t think it will be blindly obvious to anyone who hasn’t worked in the enterprise production environment

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
The adversarial part is the interesting bit and I think you are right that it is the missing piece. Right now the agent is a very fast assistant that does what you asked. It does not push back, because it has no independent evidence to push back with. If you say "buy the dip", it builds you a dip buyer.

  
What I have instead is a much dumber version of what you describe: the engine is the adversary, not another agent. It refuses to grade take-profit into the verdict, it fills at the ask and the bid rather than the midpoint, it holds back a slice of history the strategy never touched, and it returns SHELF as often as anything else. The agent proposes, the engine says no. That is one round of pushback, not the merciless stress test you are describing, but it has the advantage of being mechanical rather than another model that can be talked around.

  
The honest limit on "validating the pitch with factual evidence from verified sources": I do not have that. No news, no filings, no fundamentals beyond an earnings calendar. So an agent here can be adversarial about whether a rule survives history, and completely silent about whether the rule makes sense in the world. Those are different kinds of wrong and only one of them is covered.

  
On the 1000x, congratulations and I mean that, but I would want to know the max drawdown along the way before I drew conclusions about the system. That is the number my own curve was hiding from me until someone in this sub asked.

comments.author: konegsberg
comments.body: Ha that’s why I’ll never release my perfected 1 hour BTC bot. I know someone will catch on to the strategy and everyone will use it and kill it, but my hope is by then I’ll figure something out with weather or 15 min

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Sensible. Though for what it is worth, the thing that kills a strategy is usually not other people finding it, it is the edge being smaller than you measured. Of the seven famous strategies I ran through my own engine on real prices, five made money and two graded negative, and the two that failed are ones you can read about in any book. Being public did not kill them; they were never as good as the writeups said.

  
An hour BTC bot is at least on the right side of that. Crypto has fewer people grinding the same lookback than SPY does.

comments.author: TheeCloutGenie
comments.body: If it’s not making money smh it’s all about the prompts

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
I wanted that to be true, because the prompt is the part I can fix in an afternoon.

Counted this morning: my bots win 50.2% of 24,908 trades. Average winner $48.80. Average loser $135.09. No prompt fixes a 2.77x gap between those two — that is exit logic and position sizing, and it was wrong in every phrasing I tried. The prompt decided what to buy. The arithmetic decided what it cost.

replies.author: ZamStudio3d
replies.body: So you lost money on your own platform

comments.author: TheeCloutGenie
comments.body: Paper trading is very different than live

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Agreed, and I can name my own gap: nothing I run gets routed. No partials, no rejects, no queue position. A whole class of failure I cannot see from here.

What paper does catch is arithmetic. 892 bots, 24,908 closed trades in two weeks, 50.2% winners, down $1.06M. Live would have made that worse, not better. Cheaper to learn it this way.

comments.author: ochimaru420
comments.body: My biggest lesson the past months has been to not trust backtests and paper traders.  Simulated environments create simulated results. Claude and other AI make false assumptions about strategies and test results calling good strategies flawed and bad strategies solid all because backtest data is shallow and limited compared to live data.

comments.author: vitholomewjenkins
comments.body:
My bot trades credit spreads on SPX. It has defined rules to trigger a trade. It has Take profit and stop loss parameters. It has guardrails in place to manage risk, which will preserve capital.   
It all started with a prompt, but the production bot was honed down to repeatable rules to follow. It’s profitable now.   
All that to say, ask your AI to learn and improve on the strategy. And repeat until you are profitable or move on to the next strategy.
